title: Targeted technology coadoption for reconciling energy savings and equity gains in the residential energy transition - Nature Energy
text:
AbstractThe transition to net-zero residential energy relies on the rapid integration of photovoltaics (PV), electric vehicles and heat pumps, yet their systemic interactions remain under-examined. Using machine learning across 17,900 households, we show that targeting energy use and cost reduction leads to technology allocation to traditional early adopters—wealthy, single-family homeowners, reinforcing spatial clustering. Conversely, aiming at minimizing population-wide energy burden produces a socio-demographic realignment, directing technologies to underserved households and yielding a more spatially dispersed distribution. PV deployment to these households leads to strong equity gains relative to electric vehicles or heat pumps. Promoting co-adoption further reduce energy burden. These results underscore the need for targeted, bundled support that extends beyond homeowner-centric models to deliver PV access and integrated technology portfolios to low-income renter and multi-family sectors.

Data availability

The underlying primary datasets used in this analysis are publicly available from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) Public Use Microdata, available at https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/. Source data are provided with this paper.
Code availability

The custom simulation and analysis code developed for this study is available via GitHub at https://github.com/reconjohn/tradeoff and via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23103953 (ref. 47).
